cast.say: How hard can it be?

slides.bottom: Spoiler: harder than it looked.
Back, neck, feet… the whole set.
Sleep? Never heard of her.

cast.say: Why do nights make it hurt more?

slides.bottom: Kay had a few answers.

slides.top:
Short sleep can turn
the pain volume up.

cast.say: Less sleep, lower pain tolerance

slides.bottom: Tissues recover more slowly, too.

Blackout curtains, eye mask,
earplugs, a cool room.

slides.top:
Tip 2: Coffee early
in the shift — not before bed.
slides.bottom: Sunnies on the way home help too.

slides.top:
Tip 3: Keep strength training,
just make it smaller.
slides.bottom:
Two short sessions a week beats
a big plan that falls apart.

Shift position, take mini walks
in the long, quiet hours.

cast.say: Pain sticks around or affects sleep or work

slides.bottom:
Sleepy at the wheel or can't sleep?
Talk to your GP.

caption:
Quinn started night shifts and everything ached a bit more. Sound familiar?

Short or broken sleep can lower pain tolerance and slow recovery, so aches can feel louder on a night roster.

A few things that often help: protect your day sleep (dark, quiet, cool room), have caffeine early in the shift, keep short regular strength sessions, and move a little every hour on long shifts.

If pain hangs around or starts affecting your sleep or work, it's worth getting it looked at early. If sleepiness is affecting your driving, or sleep is a constant struggle, chat with your GP.

slides.top:
Quinn planned a road trip
AND a long flight.

cast.say: Holiday mode: ON

slides.bottom: Hours of sitting. Easy, right?

slides.top:
Hour three in the car.
The back files a complaint.
slides.bottom: And the neck co-signed it.
Neck now stiff as a plank.

cast.say: Is travel just bad for backs?

slides.bottom: Kay had a simpler answer.

cast.say: Hours in one position = stiff

slides.bottom:
Breaking up sitting beats
hunting for a perfect posture.

slides.top:
Tip 1: Set up the seat
before you go.
slides.bottom:
Knees a little bent, slight
recline, towel behind low back.

A brisk few-minute walk and
some gentle back arches.

slides.top:
Tip 3: In the air, keep
the blood moving.
slides.bottom:
Aisle walks, ankle pumps and
shoulder rolls in your seat.

Close, both hands, no twist.
Wheels whenever you can.

cast.say: Calf pain or one swollen, warm leg

slides.bottom:
Chest pain or breathlessness?
Seek medical care promptly.

caption:
A road trip plus a long flight left Quinn with a grumpy back and a very stiff neck.

Often it isn't the seat itself but the hours of staying still, so breaking up sitting tends to help more than chasing a perfect posture.

Set up your car seat before you leave (knees slightly bent, a slight recline, a towel roll behind the lower back), stop about every two hours for a short walk, keep ankles and shoulders moving on flights, and lift luggage close with both hands and no twist.

Calf pain, one swollen or warm leg, chest pain or breathlessness after travel need prompt medical care. Back pain that spreads below the knee with numbness or weakness is worth getting assessed.

Long drive,

story.body: 4 travel tips from Quinn's new reel

cast.say: Uphill? Nailed it.

slides.bottom: Now just the easy bit: down.
Every step: slam the brakes.
Thighs sore, ankles a bit wobbly.

cast.say: Why does DOWN hurt more than UP?

slides.bottom: Short answer: braking.

cast.say: Thighs brake on every step down

slides.bottom:
Kneecaps cop far more load
on steep steps than on the flat.

slides.top:
Tip 1: Train the down,
not just the distance.
slides.bottom:
Stairs, hills and slow, controlled
step-downs in the weeks before.

Single-leg work can help ankles
handle roots and loose gravel.

Weight on the hip belt; poles can
ease the braking load on knees.

slides.top:
Tip 4: Tape hot spots
before you start.
slides.bottom:
Sort socks and laces early, not
once the skin already stings.

cast.say: Can't take 4 steps, or knee swells fast

slides.bottom:
Knee locking or giving way?
Numbness that won't settle?

caption:
Quinn conquered the summit, then the walk down had the knees complaining and the next morning's stairs felt like a boss level.

On the way down, your thigh muscles act like brakes on every step, and the kneecap takes much more load on steep steps than on flat ground. That braking work is often why soreness peaks a day or two later.

Train the descent with stairs and controlled step-downs, add some single-leg balance work, carry the pack weight on the hip belt (poles can help), and tape hot spots before you set off.

An ankle you can't walk four steps on, a knee that swells quickly, locks or gives way, or numbness that won't settle is worth getting checked.

topic: Lifting at work and back pain

slides.top:
Quinn's new job: moving
boxes all day.

cast.say: Box 1: easy peasy.

slides.bottom: Strong quokka. Long shift.
It weighed less than a sandwich.

cast.think: My lifting must be all wrong…

slides.bottom: Cue a night of dramatic sighing.

cast.say: One small box did all this?

slides.bottom: Kay had a different theory.

slides.top:
It's often the dose,
not the last box.

cast.say: Load adds up over a shift

slides.bottom:
Tired muscles share load less,
so late lifts can feel the most.

Regular, progressive training
can grow your capacity.

slides.top:
Tip 2: Mix up tasks and
spread the heavy ones.
slides.bottom:
Not every big lift crammed
into the last hour.

cast.say: That trolley isn't decor!

slides.bottom:
Trolleys and lifting gear only
help if they leave the corner.

Sore doesn't always mean harm.
Many backs settle within weeks.

cast.say: Leg weakness, numbness, or after a fall

slides.bottom:
Groin numbness, bladder or bowel
changes: seek care promptly.

caption:
Quinn moved boxes all day, then a tiny box late in the shift set the back off. Quinn blamed bad technique.

Back pain at work is often more about the total load across a shift than one lift. As muscles tire, they share the work less, so a light box at the end can be the last straw.

Building strength over time, rotating tasks, spreading heavy jobs across the day, using trolleys and other aids, and staying gently active can all help. Most episodes ease within a few weeks.

Groin numbness, bladder or bowel changes, worsening leg weakness, fever, unexplained weight loss, or pain after a big fall need urgent medical assessment.

topic: Jumper's knee: why rest alone fails

cast.say: Call me Air Quinn!

slides.bottom: Three games a week. Easy.

Sore just below the kneecap.
Worse the next morning.

Back on court… and the pain
came straight back.

cast.say: I rested! Why is it back?

slides.bottom: Kay had a few answers.

slides.top:
Rest calms it down.
It doesn't build it up.

cast.say: Tendons get stronger with load

slides.bottom:
It often flares when load jumps
faster than the tendon adapts.

slides.top:
Tip 1: Settle it with
holds, not the couch.
slides.bottom:
Wall-sit style holds, 30–45 sec,
a few sets.

Slow strength work, 3x a week:
the step people often skip.

Small hops first, then higher,
faster and more.

Mild pain that settles within 24h
is often OK. Worse? Scale back.

cast.say: Swelling, locking or giving way

slides.bottom:
Or no change after months
of steady, well-run rehab.

caption:
Quinn joined a basketball comp, got a sore spot just below the kneecap, and rested for three weeks. Back on court, the pain came straight back.

Rest can calm an irritated tendon, but it doesn't make it stronger. Tendons often adapt to load, so a gradual plan tends to work better than waiting it out.

Things that often help: calming holds like wall sits, slow heavy strength work a few times a week, bringing jumping back step by step, and checking how the knee feels the next morning. Meaningful change can take a few months, so consistency matters.

If the knee swells, locks or gives way, or nothing changes after months of steady rehab, get it assessed.

topic: Coming back after a long injury

cast.say: Did you miss me?!

slides.bottom: Legs strong. Tests passed.

slides.top:
First training back.
One quick turn and…
slides.bottom:
Legs: ready.
Brain: absolutely not.
Even the stairs look suspicious.

cast.say: Strong but scared. Is that weird?

slides.bottom: Not weird at all, said Kay.

cast.say: Months of guarding teach caution

slides.bottom:
Confidence grows from proof,
not just from waiting.

Strength and hop tests vs the
other leg show what it can do.

Then unplanned moves,
then game pressure.

Small, controlled versions first,
then build it up.

Shorter minutes, easier games.
Feels off? Step back a stage.

cast.say: New or worsening pain or swelling

slides.bottom:
Struggling with fear or mood?
Talk to your GP.

caption:
Quinn spent six months out injured, passed the tests, and still froze on the first quick turn at training. Legs ready, brain not so sure.

That's common. Trust often comes back after strength does, because months of protecting a limb can teach the brain to be cautious. Confidence tends to grow from evidence rather than time alone.

What may help: strength and hop tests against the other side, reintroducing feared moves slow then fast then unplanned, practising the movement that caused the injury in small steps, and returning in stages. Your first game may feel harder than training, and that's normal.

New or worsening pain or swelling is worth checking. If fear or low mood is weighing on you, talk to your GP.

cast.say: Just one more episode.

slides.bottom: Five episodes later…
It may drift down the leg too.
Quinn's bum had opinions.

cast.say: It's my piriformis, right? I read it online.

slides.bottom: Kay wasn't so sure yet.

slides.top:
Deep bum pain has
many possible sources.

cast.say: Nerve, hamstring, hip or back can all do it

slides.bottom:
Often an irritated nerve that
doesn't love long sitting.

Cushion on hard seats, and
regular stops on long drives.

Squashing a cranky nerve can
stir it up. Gentle is fine.

Easy, comfortable movement,
no forcing big stretches.

Strong hips can share the load
so one area isn't overloaded.

cast.say: Pain below the knee, numbness or weakness

slides.bottom:
Saddle numbness, bladder or
bowel changes: urgent care.

caption:
Quinn binge-watched a whole season and stood up with a deep ache in the bum. Long drives made it worse; walking oddly helped.

Deep buttock pain is often blamed on the piriformis, but an irritated nerve, the hamstring tendon, the hip or the lower back can all cause similar pain. That's why an assessment matters.

Things that may help: break up long sitting, use a cushion on hard seats, go easy on hard ball rolling, try gentle nerve glides, and build hip and trunk strength.

Get it checked if pain travels below the knee, gets worse with coughing or bending, or comes with numbness or weakness. Saddle numbness or bladder or bowel changes need urgent medical care.

slides.bottom: Rolls over. Rolls back. Sighs.

cast.say: What even is a bursa?

slides.bottom: Kay grabbed a pen.

slides.top:
A bursa is a tiny
cushion near tendons.

cast.say: Often the tendon is the real story

slides.bottom:
It's why the name is

Uncross your legs, and try not

slides.top:
Tip 2: Build the tendon,
don't just rest it.
slides.bottom:
Gradual strength work,
step by step, with a plan.

Steady weeks, no sudden

Padding and changing positions
take pressure off the knee.

cast.say: Hot, red, swollen with fever? Same day

slides.bottom:
Pain lingering or getting worse?
Worth a proper assessment.

caption:
Quinn googled a sore hip, read "bursitis" and the panic was instant. Hip sore at night, legs crossed at the desk all day… sound familiar?

A bursa is a small fluid-filled cushion that helps tendons glide. In the hip and shoulder the tendon is often the bigger part of the picture.

What may help: ease the squeeze (uncross your legs, avoid sleeping on the sore side), build tendon strength gradually instead of only resting, keep weekly activity steady, and use padding if you kneel a lot.

A hot, red, swollen area with fever needs same-day medical care. Pain that lingers or worsens is worth getting assessed.

topic: Stiff big toe and turf toe

cast.say: 20 km? Easy.

slides.bottom: Training starts today!
Every push-off: ouch.
Floppy slippers: also a no.

cast.say: Why does my big toe hate walking?

slides.bottom: Kay had a look.

slides.top:
Each step ends with
the toe bending up.

cast.say: A stiff joint makes push-off sore

slides.bottom:
Often it's arthritis in that
joint, coming on gradually.

Less bend at the toe can mean
a more comfortable push-off.

Stronger push-off muscles can
help, even if range doesn't.

Long walks and hills load the
toe most. Add them slowly.

Pushing a stiff joint into pain
tends to stir it up.

cast.say: Toe bent back hard and can't take weight

slides.bottom:
Also: big swelling, a changed
shape, or pain limiting your day.

caption:
Quinn signed up for a charity walk, and by week two the big toe had opinions. Barefoot at home? Even worse.

Every step ends with the big toe bending up to push off. When that joint is stiff (often from gradual arthritis), push-off can get sore. Turf toe is different: a sprain from the toe being bent back hard.

Things that often help: stiffer-soled shoes, calf and foot strengthening, building walking distance and hills gradually, and not forcing a stiff toe into painful stretches.

If the toe was bent back hard and won't take weight, or there's big swelling or a change in shape, get it checked. Pain that limits your day is worth assessing too.

slides.bottom: Kay asked about the whole week.

cast.say: Throwing outran what it could handle

Too much, too soon, too often
can add up fast.

Watch for preseason spikes
and playing for two teams.

slides.top:
Tip 2: Strengthen the
cuff and shoulder blade.
slides.bottom:
Back-of-shoulder work, and

slides.top:
Tip 3: Power starts in
the legs and trunk.
slides.bottom:
When hips and trunk do their

Mid-back rotation can take

slides.top:
Tip 5: After a break,
ease back in stages.
slides.bottom:
Build distance and effort slowly.
No full-power 'test' throws.

cast.say: Lost speed, dead arm, or sore past 2 days

slides.bottom:
Young thrower with elbow pain?
Stop throwing and get assessed.

caption:
Quinn joined two cricket teams, threw everything in preseason, and by week three the shoulder said no thanks.

Throwing shoulders often get sore when load outpaces what the shoulder can handle, rather than from one weak muscle. Sudden preseason spikes and playing for several teams are common setups.

What may help: track throws and plan rest days, strengthen the rotator cuff and shoulder blade, let the legs and trunk share the work, keep the mid-back mobile, and return after a break in stages.

Get it checked if you notice lost speed or accuracy, a dead arm feeling, or soreness lasting beyond a day or two. Young throwers with elbow pain should stop throwing and get assessed.
